question: Random checks introduced in recent months on trucks carrying waste from France to Spain have detected serious or very serious infractions on one in every three of those vehicles. It is common practice to hide waste that should have been processed in the country of origin among treated waste and other waste that can be transported legally.

These practices are driven by the fact that treating waste in Spain costs a sixth of what it does in France, meaning big profits for companies that transport waste in this way rather than collecting and treating it where it was produced. The method used results in untreated, highly polluting waste being buried in landfills at the destination.
Although oversight of this process is ultimately up to national authorities, the cross-border nature of this ‘business’ calls for EU intervention. 1.
What information does the Commission have on these non-compliant operations?
What scope does the Commission have to encourage better cooperation among Member States to deal with such practices?
Does the Commission believe that current legislation is enough to put a stop to these practices?
answer: The Commission was not aware of the case mentioned by the Honourable Member and has not taken specific action on it but will reach out to the competent authorities in the Member States concerned. Addressing waste trafficking is a priority for the EU overall policy against organised crime and the protection of the environment, including in the new Environmental Crime Directive (1).

Actions are taken to improve cooperation between enforcement agencies from the Member States, as well as with the EU Network for the Implementation and Enforcement of Environmental Law (2), Europol and international organisations (3).

The EU is also providing significant financial support to operational projects which are directly targeting waste trafficking, focusing on particular waste streams like plastic waste or e-waste, as well as on coordination with third countries (4). The new EU regulation on waste shipments (5) lays down new rules designed to reinforce the EU response against waste trafficking.

Firstly, it establishes an EU ‘waste shipment enforcement group’ to further increase cooperation between environmental, customs, police and other relevant national inspection authorities, as well as EU and international law enforcement networks. Secondly, it empowers the Commission, through the European Anti-Fraud Office, to support transnational investigations by Member States on waste trafficking.

Thirdly, it strengthens rules on inspections and penalties against illegal shipments of waste. Common criteria for determining the types and levels of penalties to be imposed for infringements will make penalties more deterrent and consistent across the EU. Enforcement by national authorities is essential to ensure the effectiveness of EU rules.
